# P R E F A C E ,
## On the usefulness of this book.

I have often wondered not a little that men, who have left almost no subject untouched in their writings, have not yet composed a Chemical Library <term>Library: Borel uses the Latin *Bibliotheca* to mean a "bibliography"—a comprehensive catalog of books and authors—rather than a physical room filled with books.</term>; therefore, moved by the persuasion of friends, I have applied my effort to this, and I have obtained a greater number of authors than I had promised myself, and I am still discovering more daily, so much so that I hope I shall soon give you the second part of this Bibliography, and in a better order, namely chronologically, and with short biographies <note>original: *vitis compendiosis*</note> of the principal authors; for I shall always collect authors in the future,

<meta>catchword: therefore</meta>

<summary>This page concludes Pierre Borel's dedication and opens his preface, where he expresses surprise at the lack of a comprehensive chemical bibliography and announces his intention to expand this work with a second, chronological volume.</summary>

# PREFACE.

I beseech all the curious <note>In the 17th century, "curious" (*curiosos*) referred to serious scholars and researchers who were "careful" or "diligent" in their investigations.</note> who set their hands to this work, that they deign to communicate to me those things which are missing from my book; for if they so desire, such additions will be published in their own name for the sake of their honor.

The use of this work is manifold, although I have heard that some have already been grumbling <note>original: *obgannivisse* — literally "to have snarled" or "yelped like a dog," suggesting petty or mindless criticism.</note> that it will be useless. In saying this, they do an injury to Conrad Gessner, Lycosthenes, Simler, Draudius, Du Verdier, Vignier, Antonides van der Linden, Du Chesne, Paschalius, and countless other weavers of similar Libraries <term>Library: Borel refers to the Latin *Bibliotheca*, which in this context means a "bibliography" or a universal catalog of books, not a physical building.</term>.

Firstly, it will be useful to those devoted to the Chemical art <note>The term *Chimica* at this time encompassed both what we now call chemistry and the esoteric pursuits of alchemy.</note>; for nothing should remain hidden from exquisite researchers, and what is incomplete in one book is completed in another, and thus they will be able to see the consensus of all Authors. Furthermore, they usually cannot request an Author from booksellers if his name is unknown. And whereas Trevisan <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490) was a famous alchemist who reportedly traveled for years and spent a fortune searching for rare hermetic texts.</note> once asserted that he only reached his desired goal late in life due to a scarcity of books, seekers of that art will no longer be able to complain of this matter.

Secondly, when anyone desires to become thoroughly acquainted with the Authors who have formally discussed a certain mineral or other Chemical subject, he will easily find the desired items in this little book, since I have composed an alphabetical index both by the principal subjects and by names.

<summary>Borel defends the utility of his chemical bibliography against critics and explains how it helps scholars find rare texts and identify consensus among alchemical authors.</summary>
<keywords>bibliography, alchemy, chemistry, Conrad Gessner, Bernard of Trevisan, book collecting, scientific indices, history of science</keywords>

# PREFACE.

Thirdly, if anyone desires to know all the works of a certain Author held in delight above all others, along with his various editions, he will find these also in this list, its Appendix, and the Corollary.

Fourthly, our work will also be useful to Librarians, for filling the book cabinets with selected and choice books.

Fifthly, it will bring both learning (since with this Catalog they will come to know *Chemical* books <note>In Borel's time, "Chemical" (*Chimicos*) referred to both practical chemistry and the esoteric study of alchemy.</note> previously unknown to them) and profit to Booksellers; for it will increase the number of buyers, who often, due to a lack of Authors' names or ignorance of editions, either do not buy books or cannot find them.

Sixthly, this great crowd of Philosophers will be no small proof of the truth of *Alchemy*; and since *Ventura* <note>Laurentius Ventura was a 16th-century Venetian alchemist and physician.</note>, *Maier* <note>Michael Maier (1568–1622) was a celebrated German physician and counselor to Emperor Rudolf II, known for his alchemical writings and emblems.</note>, and others boast of naming three hundred Authors, I leave you as the judge of our labor <note>Borel suggests that his own list is significantly larger than the three hundred names cited by previous authorities, thereby providing even stronger evidence for the validity of the alchemical tradition.</note>.

Seventhly, this work will also be most welcome to Authors still enjoying the breath of life <note>original: *vitali fruentibus aura* — a poetic idiom meaning those who are still living.</note>, or to their sons, since they will see in it a List <term>List: Borel uses *Elenchus*, meaning a structured index or register.</term> of their works, by which it will be clear throughout the world that they have devoted their labor to this matter.

Eighthly, there exist countless men among foreign nations who have not heard that *French* books exist, and countless in *France* who have not heard of the books of other nations; however, through our Catalog, all authors will become known to all people, of whom

Ninthly, it will be useful not only for **Alchemy**, but also regarding mineral matters and the secrets of Authors, or for the curious.

Tenthly, if anyone desires to create a corpus of **Chemical Authors** <note>original: "Authorum Chimicorum"</note>—for example, the Egyptians, Hebrews, Arabs, Syrians, Chaldeans, Persians, Greeks, Gauls, Germans, Swiss, Poles, English, Italians, Spaniards, etc., or of Poets, of women, etc.—he will easily be able to pluck all their names from here. ## *Privilege* of the King.

By the Grace and **Privilege** <note>In the 17th century, a "Privilege" was a form of early copyright. It was an exclusive legal right granted by the monarch to an author or printer, protecting the work from being pirated by others for a specific number of years.</note> of the King, given at Paris on the tenth day of November 1653. Signed, By the King in his Council, **PELISSON** <note>Paul Pellisson (1624–1693) was a prominent French historian and official who served as a secretary to King Louis XIV.</note>: Permission is granted to **PIERRE BOREL**, Physician of Castres, to have printed by whichever Bookseller he deems fit, a Book, entitled, ***Chemical Library, or Catalogue of Hermetic Philosophical Books, etc.*** <note>original Latin: "Bibliotheca Chimica, seu Catalogus Librorum Philosophicorum Hermeticorum, &c."</note> During the time and space of five years, counting from the day it shall be finished printing. Strictly forbidding...

**Abenragel**, also cited as an alchemist. <note>likely referring to the Arab astrologer and astronomer Abenragel, also known as Albohazen Haly filius Abenragel (10th-11th century).</note>
**Abmimazar**, cited in the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (Rosary of the Philosophers), a key 16th-century alchemical text.</note> with illustrations; he is perhaps the same person as **Albumazar**.
**Abraham the Jew**, mentioned by Flamel, where certain excerpts from him are seen. <note>Referring to the legendary "Book of Abraham the Jew" which Nicolas Flamel supposedly discovered and spent decades deciphering to learn the secret of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>
I saw a manuscript by the same author, with illustrations and a certain explanation, in Paris, in quarto format. <note>original: "Lutetiæ in 4." Quarto refers to the size of the book, made by folding a full sheet of paper twice to create four leaves.</note>
The same author wrote on the **Cabalistic art**.
**Abraham of Portaleone** <note>original: "Abrahainus è portu leonis." Abraham ben David Portaleone (1542–1612) was a Jewish physician and scholar from Mantua.</note> published three books on gold at Venice in 1586, in quarto, printed by Porta.
To **Abraham** is also attributed a chemical book called the *Yetzirah* <note>original: "Ietſira." The *Sefer Yetzirah* (Book of Creation) is a primary text of Jewish mysticism, which Renaissance alchemists often interpreted through a chemical lens.</note>, which is extremely obscure.
**Abrisius**. According to Quercetanus, he is a Chemist. <note>Quercetanus is the Latinized name of Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent physician and chemist who advocated for the ideas of Paracelsus.</note>
**Abubasa**, wrote *The Vinegar of the Philosophers*.
**Abuhali**, or Hasen the son of Hali, is an alchemist. <note>Likely referring to the famous Persian polymath Avicenna (Ibn Sina), whose full name was Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Abd Allah ibn Sina.</note>
**Accursius** the commentator, on the *Rosary* of Arnold, according to the report of Nasari. <note>Referring to a commentary on the works of the famous alchemist Arnold of Villanova.</note>
**Achiratus**, cited by Hortulanus. <note>Hortulanus, or "The Gardener," was a 14th-century commentator on the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus.</note>
**Acratus**, cited in the Latin *Turba*. <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between various ancient philosophers.</note>
**Acsubofen**, **Acsubofes**, or **Acsubofer**, is praised in the Latin *Turba*.
**Actomanus**, a Chemist.
**Actorienes**, a writer of Chemistry according to Hortulanus.
**Actor** is a Chemist, according to Senior. <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arab alchemist whose works were highly influential in Europe.</note>
The treatise of **Adabefis**, concerning how the alchemy of the sun and moon is performed, according to the report of Nasari. <note>In alchemical code, the "Sun" and "Moon" typically refer to Gold and Silver.</note>

### CHEMICAL WORKS

**Adalmos**, from Plato. <note>Alchemical texts often attributed ancient philosophical authority to legendary figures like Adalmos through the lens of Plato.</note>
**Adam**, from the illustrated *Rosary*. <note>original: "Rosario figurato." This refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise known for its symbolic woodcut illustrations.</note>
**The Son of Adam**, is listed in the *Crowd*. <note>original: "turba." Refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a fictional gathering of philosophers.</note>

**Adomat**, from the third book of the Anonymous author. He is a Chemist.

**Cardinal Adrian**, See **Dastin**. <note>John Dastin was an influential 14th-century English alchemist who wrote famous letters to Pope John XXII and Cardinal Adrian.</note>
**Adros the Arab**.
**Adrox** (perhaps **Adrop**) of the Philosophers. In German. <note>term: <term>Adrop</term> refers to the "Philosophical Lead" or the raw material of the Great Work.</note>
**Egidius de Vadis**, *Dialogue between Nature and the Son of Art*.
By the same author, a table of various metals, in the *Chemical Theater*. <note>original: "Theatro Chemico." This was a massive multi-volume compendium of alchemical writings published in the early 17th century.</note>
The same is found with the treatise by Penotus on *Hidden Chemical Matters*, Frankfurt Edition, 1595, octavo. <note>Bernard Georges Penot was a French physician and alchemist; "octavo" refers to the book's size, created by folding a printed sheet three times to form eight leaves.</note>
**B. Egidius the Hermit**.
**Egidius, Master of the Hospital**, who wrote a book on 125 (perhaps it should read only 12) stones; according to the illustrated *Rosary*, he is a Chemist. Others separate these names and read **Egidius** and the **Master of the Hospital** as two different people.
**Aegistus**, cited in the *Dismissed Word* by Trevisan. <note>original: "Verbo dimiſſo." A reference to Trevisan's work *Le Parole Délaissée*.</note>
**Aelia Laelia Crispis**. The Bolognese Epitaph explained by Richard White of Basingstoke. <note>original: "Richardus vitus Bastinstochius." The Aelia Laelia Crispis is a famous, mysterious riddle-epitaph found in Bologna that many alchemists attempted to interpret as a chemical recipe.</note>

### CHEMISTRY 23

**The Revelation of the Secret Spirit**, with Commentary. Published in London. <note>original: "Apocalypsis Spiritus secreti." In an alchemical context, an "apocalypse" refers to the uncovering or unveiling of hidden natural secrets.</note>

**Wisdom of the Ancients**, concerning the **Philosopher's Stone**, and the cure of diseases, with forty hieroglyphic figures. Manuscript. <note>original: "Sapientia veterum, de lapide Philosophorum." Alchemists believed their "Stone" could not only transmute metals but also act as a universal medicine or panacea.</note>

**A Collection concerning the Dew**, Manuscript. <note>original: "de Rore." Dew was highly prized by alchemists (specifically "Philosophical Dew") as a pure, celestial source of the "universal spirit" used in the initial stages of the Great Work.</note>

**A Useful Work**, Manuscript.

**A Defense of the Most Secret Art**, and Introductory Remarks, with ancient writers of Alchemy. Basel, folio edition, 1561. <note>original: "Artis Secretissimæ defensio." Basel was a primary center for the printing of Hermetic and Paracelsian texts in the 16th century.</note>

The *Albedo* (whiteness) is the second major stage of the alchemical process, following the blackness of decay, and represents the washing or purification of the matter.</note>

**On the Inquirers of Philosophy**, Manuscript. <note>original: "Des Inquisiteurs de Philosophie" (French). This refers to seekers of the "True Philosophy" or alchemy.</note>

**A Chemical Book**, where the signs of the Zodiac are found. <note>original: "Liure Chimique" (French). Alchemical operations were often timed according to astrological cycles, as each metal was believed to be governed by a specific planet and celestial house.</note>

**The Chemical Wedding**, in German. <note>original: "Nuptiæ Chimicæ, Germanicè." This likely refers to *The Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz*, a seminal Rosicrucian text published in 1616.</note>

**Six Most Ancient Writings of Chemical Philosophy**.

**Anonymous on the Generation of Metals**, in the *Hermetic Museum*. <note>original: "Musæo Hermetico." This refers to a famous collection of alchemical tracts first published in Frankfurt; it served as a standard reference for the "Hermetic science."</note>

**A Work on Stones**, Manuscript. <note>original: "Opus Lapidum."</note>

**The Author of the "Splendor of the Sun."** <note>original: "Splendoris Solis." This is one of the most famous and lavishly illuminated alchemical manuscripts, containing a series of twenty-two allegorical paintings.</note>

**The Book of the Philosophers' Aurora**. <note>original: "Aureliæ Philosophorum." The *Aurora* (dawn) symbolizes the transition to the final "red" stage of the Great Work and the birth of the golden stone.</note>

**The Book of the Golden Cymbals**. <note>original: "Cymbali Aurei liber."</note>

# BIBLIOTHECA

Author of the **Great Rosary**. <note>original: "Rosarij Magni." The *Rosarium Philosophorum* is one of the most famous alchemical texts, known for its series of twenty woodcuts depicting the symbolic marriage of the King and Queen.</note>
**Children’s Play**. <note>original: "Ludus Puerorum." A common title in alchemical literature, suggesting that once the secret of the "Stone" is understood, the actual labor is as easy as child's play.</note>

**Brother Anselm**, see Lacinio. <note>original: "Frater Anselmus, vide Lacinium." Referring to Janus Lacinius, who edited the works of Petrus Bonus and other medieval masters.</note>

The term *crambe* (literally "cabbage") refers to a rehashed or tedious argument. This entry relates to the "Antimony War," a fierce 17th-century medical debate in Paris over the use of chemical vs. traditional medicines.</note>

**Observations on Jean Antaruetus’ Apology for Alchemy**, Frankfurt.

**On Antimony**: Written by Alexander von Suchten, Sala, Kerner, Codronchus, Stenglius, Philologus, Toxites, Greuer, Basil Valentine, Chartier, and many others. <note>original: "De Antimonio." **Anthony of Paris**, **The Common Way**, cited by Nazari. <note>original: "Via Vilis." Literally "The Cheap Way," referring to a method of making the Stone using common or inexpensive materials.</note>

**Anthony**, cited by an anonymous author on the **Mass of the Sun**. <note>original: "de Massa Solis."</note>

**Master Anthony** on the **Philosopher's Stone**.

**The Rebis, and the Governance of Fire**, with Rhenanus. <note>original: "Rebis, & Regimine ignis, cum Rhenano." The *Rebis* is a central alchemical symbol of the "divine hermaphrodite," representing the union of opposites. Johannes Rhenanus was a 17th-century German physician and chemist.</note>

**The Golden Tree**, along with Pierre-Jean Fabre’s **Triumphal Chariot of Antimony** by [Basilius] Valentinus, with notes by the same Fabre. <note>original: "Arbor Aurea, cum P. Ioh. Fabri curru triumphali Antimonii Valentini." Pierre-Jean Fabre was a 17th-century physician who integrated alchemy into medicine.</note>
**On the Most Secret Mystery of the Ancient Philosophers**, octavo edition, 1612.

# BIBLIOGRAPHY

**Arnold the Greek**, in the Preface to the *Book of the Apple*, cited by Aristotle, concerning the **Philosopher’s Stone**. <note>original: "Arnoldus Græcus, in Proœmio libri de Pomo, citatus ab Aristotele, de lapide Philos." The *Book of the Apple* (*Liber de Pomo*) was a popular medieval text falsely attributed to Aristotle, depicting him on his deathbed discussing the immortality of the soul while inhaling the scent of an apple.</note>

**Arras** in the *Assembly of the Philosophers*. <note>original: "Arras in Turba Philos." The *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate among ancient sages.</note>

A metallurgical process using corrosive substances to purify gold of its impurities.</note>, etc. <note>The author likely means Augustus, Elector of Saxony, who was a renowned patron of alchemy; the attribution to Bavaria may be an error in the source text.</note>.

**The Princes of the Chemical Art**: **Avicenna** and **Geber**; the former of whom has never appeared until now, while the latter is published augmented with figures <note>referring to woodcut illustrations of laboratory equipment</note>. Basel, 1572, octavo.

**Avicenna’s** *Nine Distinctions*.

**The same author’s** *The Gate of Elements*, a chemical book. Basel, 1572, octavo.

**Avicenna’s** or **Abohali’s** (that is, Father Hali), *Epistle to King Hasem on the Correct Matter* <note>original: "de re recta."</note>, in the *Chemical Theater* <note>The *Theatrum Chemicum* was a massive multi-volume compendium of alchemical literature published in the 17th century.</note>.

**The same author’s** *Declaration of the Philosophers’ Stone*, addressed to his son Abohali; in the same volume.

**The same author’s** *Book on the Freezing of Stones and Minerals*, published with the *Blare of the Trumpet* <note>original: "Clangore Buccinæ," a common title for alchemical tracts suggesting a "wake-up call" to the truth.</note>.

**The same author’s** *Letter to Hasten on the Correct Matter*.

<header>BIBLIOGRAPHY</header>

Commentary on **Fernelius**. <note>original: "Comment. in Fernelium"; Jean Fernel was a renowned French physician whose works on physiology and pathology were standard texts in the 16th and 17th centuries</note>

**Ferrarius**, a Chemist, praised in the *Illustrated Rose Garden*. <note>original: "in Rosario figurato"; this refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, one of the most famous alchemical manuscripts, known for its series of twenty symbolic woodcuts illustrating the "chemical wedding"</note>

The complete treatise of **Brother Ferrarius**; for until now it had been issued only in a fragmented form, published by the effort of **Combachius** alongside other Chemical Authors, 1647, in duodecimo. **Marsilio Ficino**, *On the Threefold Prolonging of Life* <note>original: "de vita tripliciter proroganda"; Ficino was the leader of the Florentine Academy and a key figure of the Renaissance who sought to combine medicine, music, and astral magic to ensure the health of scholars</note>, in octavo.

By the same author, *On the Mystery of the Golden Fleece* <note>original: "de Aurei Velleris mysterio"; in alchemical literature, the "Golden Fleece" of Jason and the Argonauts was frequently interpreted as a code for the secret of making gold</note>.

Turquetum Medicum"; referring to Sir Theodore de Mayerne, an influential Huguenot physician who served the English royal court and possessed a vast collection of medical and chemical manuscripts</note>

**Benedictus Figulus**, *The Golden Hermetic Paradise* <note>original: "Paradisus Aureolus Hermeticus"</note>, in which it is demonstrated when the golden apples of the Hesperides are to be plucked from the blessed philosophical tree. Frankfurt, 1600, in quarto. <note>Figulus was a radical Paracelsian author; the "apples of the Hesperides" is a classical metaphor used here to describe the final stage of the alchemical process</note>

**Figulus**, *The Little Olympic Garden* <note>original: "Hortulus Olympicus"</note>, in German.

By the same author, *Pandora of Natural Wonders* <note>original: "Pandora Magnalium naturalium"</note>, concerning the mystery of the Philosopher's Stone.

By the same author, *The Little Olympic Treasury* <note>original: "Thesaurinella Olympica"</note>.

By the same author, *Light in the Darkness of Lull* <note>original: "Lux, in tenebris Lullij"</note>. <note>This title suggests a clarifying commentary on the notoriously difficult works attributed to the medieval philosopher and alchemist Ramon Lull</note>

By the same author, *The Great Secret* <note>original: "Secretum Magnum"</note>.

**Johann Vincent Finck**, *Hermetic-Dogmatic Handbook* <note>original: "Enchiridium Hermetico Dogmaticum"</note>, 1626, in sextodecimo. Leipzig.

...[the messa]ger, in verse, with the Annotations of Jacques Gohory. <note>original: "en vers, avec les Annotations de Gohory"; Gohory was a 16th-century French polymath who promoted Paracelsian ideas and helped establish a "Lyceum" for chemical study in Paris.</note>

**Jacques Fontane**, *On the Art of Separation, or Spagyric Pharmacy*. <note>original: "de arte separatoria, siue Pharmacia Spagirica"; "Spagyric" is a term coined by Paracelsus, referring to the process of separating and recombining the constituents of a substance to create potent medicines.</note>

**Largus**, a writer on chemistry.

**Lafan**, a writer on chemistry, from the anonymous work *On the Mass of the Sun* <note>original: *de Massa Solis*; in alchemy, "Sol" or "the Sun" refers to Gold</note>.

*Three Treatises on the Most Secret Mystery of the Ancient Philosophers for Transmutation* <note>original: *Tres tractatus de secretissimo Antiquorum Philosophorum Arcano ad transmut.*</note>, which contains the work of **Lasnioro**, a treatise by **Arnald of Villanova**, and **Nehusius** on the *Brothers of the Rose Cross* <note>original: *Fratribus Rosæ Crucis*, referring to the Rosicrucians</note>, published at Hanau, 1618.

A *Defense of Galenic Medicine against the Slanders of Angelo Sala the Chemist* <note>original: *defensio Med. Galenic. aduersus Calumnias Angeli Salæ Chimici*</note> by **Henricus Lavater**.

*The Book of Washings* <note>original: *Livre des Lavamens*</note>, from **Lagneus**, perhaps the same as the work by **Flamel** <note>Nicolas Flamel, the famous legendary alchemist</note> titled *The Washings* <note>original: *Les Laveures*</note>.

*The Perfect and Practical Work* <note>original: "Oeuure parfaite , & pratique"</note>, according to Lull, which he had obtained from Paganus, Manuscript.

<margin>+</margin> Lull’s most useful book, *On Mercury Alone*.

Lull’s *Medical Letters*, with the *Medical Chest* <note>original: "cista Medica"; likely a compendium of remedies or a portable medical guide.</note>, are available from Johann Hornung, Nuremberg, 1625, in quarto <note>A book size where each sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>.

<margin>+</margin> *The Vade Mecum* <note>Latin for "Go with me"; a handbook or pocket guide.</note>, or *Abridgment of the Chemical Art*, along with **Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, now believed to be a pseudonym for Johann Thölde.</note>, at Paris, 1627, published by Charles Hulpeau.

Plentiful ancient manuscripts of Lull exist in the Oxford Library, according to **Combachius** <note>Johann Combach (1585–1651), a German philosopher and editor of alchemical texts.</note> in his commentary on **Ripley** <note>Sir George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), one of England’s most famous alchemists.</note>, where he reports things to be remembered about the life of Lull, drawn from the journey of **Father Pacificus** <note>Pacificus of Provins (1588–1648), a Capuchin friar and traveler.</note> to Persia in the year 1628. For there he speaks of a statue of the blessed Lull, which is still seen on the island of Mallorca, in which there are Lullist Canons publicly reading his works and preserving his relics; however, he was overwhelmed by stones <note>He was martyred by stoning while preaching in North Africa.</note> in Africa after 145 years had passed, by the power of the Elixir <note>A reference to the alchemical legend that Lull used his "Universal Medicine" to extend his life far beyond a normal span.</note>.

I hear that even in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note> there are certain curious individuals who possess a list of four thousand books by Lull, though these pertain to various sciences.

*The New Chemical Light* of the **Cosmopolite** <note>A pseudonym for Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist whose work "Novum Lumen Chymicum" was highly influential.</note>.

(Though some attribute these to **Michael Sendivogius** <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist and diplomat.</note>, they do so incorrectly, even if it seems to be confirmed by a double anagram—since he made those writings his own). He is that noble Pole, also called the **Northern Sun-Beetle** <note>original: "Heliocantharus Borealis." An alchemical moniker suggesting a creature that rolls the "sun" or gold of the north.</note>. However, I have learned through secret tradition <note>original: "Cabalistice." Here referring to oral or esoteric reports rather than Jewish Kabbalah.</note> that he was an **Englishman** <note>Likely referring to Alexander Seton (d. 1604), a Scotsman often called "the Cosmopolite" who was imprisoned for his alchemical secrets.</note>, whose heir to the **Physical Powder** <note>A common term for the Philosopher's Stone in powder form.</note> and writings was Sendivogius the Pole, who married the man’s widow. 

The true **Cosmopolite** produced twelve chapters under the name *The New Chemical Light*, an *Epilogue*, and a *Parable*; these are his genuine works. However, the following works are not considered his, but rather those of Sendivogius:

**The Cosmopolite’s** *Dialogue of the Alchemist with Mercury and Nature.*

By the same author, *A Treatise on Sulfur*.

These have been printed many times and are found alongside the *Miracles* of **Muller**, and works by **Beguin**, the *Quintessences* of **Drebbel**, and **Angurello**. They appear both as standalone volumes and in the *Chemical Theater* <note>original: "Theatro Chimico," the largest and most famous compendium of alchemical texts in the 17th century.</note>, where more corrected versions exist. They were also published in Paris, 1609, by Ruellius, in sextodecimo <note>A small book size where the paper is folded to create 16 leaves.</note>; and in Cologne, 1613, in duodecimo <note>A pocket-sized book format.</note>, by Anton Boetzer.

<header>CHEMISTRY. SECTION M</header>

By the same author, *The Philosophical Week* <note>original: "Septimana Philosophica."</note>, which contains golden enigmas concerning every kind of nature. These are proposed and unraveled in the manner of a dialogue between the most wise Solomon, King of the Israelites, the Queen of Sheba from Arabia, and Hiram, Prince of Tyre. Throughout the work, the causes of natural things—new yet true, and consistent with both reason and experience—are explained and demonstrated. It includes copperplate engravings <note>original: "figuris Cupro incisis."</note> added for each individual day. Frankfurt: [published] by Lucas Jennis, in quarto.

The same author, *On the Squared Physical Circle* <note>original: "De Circulo Phisico quadrato."</note>—that is, on gold and its medicinal virtue, which lies hidden like a kernel beneath a hard shell <note>The "hard shell" refers to the physical form of the metal, while the "kernel" is the concentrated spiritual or medicinal essence sought by alchemists.</note>. It explores whether and what kind of medicine should be sought from it. [Published] by Lucas Jennis and Johann Janson, 1616, in quarto.

<margin>Very rare and expensive</margin>
*By the same author, Michael Maier, Physician to the Emperor <note>Maier served as the personal physician and counselor to Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II, a great patron of the occult sciences.</note>, *The Most Secret Secrets* <note>original: "Arcana Arcanissima."</note>, which are the Egypto-Greek Hieroglyphics. This work aims to demonstrate that the origin of the false gods, goddesses, heroes, animals, and rituals accepted as sacred among the Ancients was actually derived from a single Egyptian artifice <term>artifice: in this context, a specific chemical or alchemical process</term> which produced a golden medicine for the mind and body, etc. London, 1614, in quarto.

<margin>Very good</margin>
+By the same author, *Atalanta Fleeing* <note>original: "Atalanta fugiens." This is Maier's most famous work, an "emblem book" that combined text, imagery, and musical scores.</note>, that is, new Emblems concerning the secrets of nature and Chemistry. Oppenheim: [published] by Johann Theodor de Bry, 1618, in quarto.

**Noscus**, a Chemist, appears in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original Latin: "in turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts</note> (according to Trevisan <note>Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist</note>) and was the King of Albania.

# BIBLIOGRAPHY

*The Council of Marriage concerning the Mass of the Sun and the Moon* <note>original Latin: "Consilij Coniugij de massa Solis & Lunæ". This refers to the alchemical "chemical wedding" or union of gold (the Sun) and silver (the Moon)</note>, Strasbourg <note>original Latin: "Argentorati"</note>, 1566, in octavo.

**Orfulus**, an author on chemical matters; he is the same as **Autumo**, as well as **Orfolcus**, **Orfoltus**, (appearing as **Orfolcus** in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original Latin: "turba Phil."; the "Turba Philosophorum" is one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts</note>) and **Orfultus**.

**Orphanus**, a writer on alchemy, according to **Petrus Bonus** <note>An Italian alchemist of the 14th century, known for his work "The Precious New Pearl"</note>.

**Orpheus**, the Greek Poet, writing on stones and gems.
By the same author, the *Argonautica*, published by **Henri Estienne** in Paris.
By the same author, the *Hymns*; this author is moreover numbered among the chemists by **Flamel** and many others.

*Discourse on Potable Gold* <note>original French: "Discours de l'Or Potable". Potable or "drinkable" gold was a legendary medicinal elixir</note> by an anonymous author.

**Master Ortholanus**, the *True Practice of Alchemy*, proven and tested in Paris in the year 1358; found in the *Chemical Theater* <note>The "Theatrum Chemicum", a massive compendium of alchemical literature</note>.

**Orthophales**, cited in the *Twelve Gates of Alchemy* <note>A seminal poem by the English alchemist George Ripley</note>.

**Ortomanus**, on monetary matters <note>original Latin: "de re Nomaria"</note>.

***The Garden of Love*** <note>original Latin: "Ortus Amoris"</note>, a book of alchemy.

**Osiander**. See **Polyander**.

**Osthanes** the Greek, according to **Ripley**, though others say he was Egyptian; a chemical writer <note>Osthanes was a legendary figure from antiquity often cited as a primary source of alchemical wisdom</note>.

**Osthares**, perhaps the same as the preceding.

**Rudolf Otreb**, a Briton (that is, **Robert Fludd** <note>An influential English Paracelsian physician, mathematician, and mystic</note>), *A Theological-Philosophical Treatise on Life, Death, and Resurrection*, dedicated to the **Brothers of the Rosy Cross** <note>The Rosicrucians, a secret society of mystics and alchemists</note>, Oppenheim, 1617, in quarto.

**Bernard Penot**, of Port-Sainte-Marie in Aquitaine: *Various treatises on the true preparation, dosage, and use of chemical medicines* <note>original: "de vera præparatione, Dosi, & vsu, Medicamentorum Chimicorum"</note>, found in the *Chemical Theater* <note>original: "Theatro Chimico"; a massive and influential multi-volume compendium of alchemical writings first published in 1602</note>, and at Frankfurt, from the shop of Johannes Rhodius, 1600, in octavo <note>A book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves</note>.

**By the same author**: *Three questions on physical Mercury* <note>original: "de corporali Mercurio"</note>, exploring whether Mercury extracted from "perfect bodies" <note>likely referring to gold or silver</note> by art contributes to the generation of the [Philosopher’s] stones; in the *Chemical Theater*.

**By the same author**: *Response to various questions*, in the same place.

**By the same author**: *57 Canons* <note>original: "Canones"; rules or foundational principles of the art</note>, in the same place.

**By the same author**: *The true extraction of Mercury from gold*, in the same place.

**By the same author**: *Axioms*.

**By the same author**: *The Medical Denarius* <note>original: "Denarium Medicum"; likely a collection of ten medical or chemical secrets or a specific weight/dosage treatise</note>. Bern, 1608, in octavo.

**By the same author**: *The Collected Works of Isaac Hollandus and Ripley’s Twelve Gates* <note>Penot edited the works of these two famous earlier alchemists: the Dutchman Isaac Hollandus and the Englishman George Ripley</note>.

*The Defense of Bernard Penot* <note>original: "Apologia"</note> against the writing of **Joseph Michelius**, concerning the matter of the Physician's Stone, its signs, and the multiple [degrees of] fire. Frankfurt, 1600, in octavo.

**Penot’s Works**, in quarto <note>A book size where each sheet is folded into four leaves</note>.

The dialogue *Chrysorrhoas* <note>Greek for "The Golden Stream"</note>, or *On the Chemical Art*, is also attributed to him.

**The same author**:
*On Potable Gold* <note>An elixir made from dissolved gold, believed to have universal healing properties</note>.
*On the Panacea* <note>The "cure-all" medicine sought by alchemists</note>.
*On Saltpeter* <note>original: "De Sale Nitro"; potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in chemical experiments and gunpowder</note>.
*On the Preparation of Tartar, etc.* <note>Tartar is a potassium salt found in wine casks, frequently used in early modern chemistry</note>.

**Zachariah a Puteo** <note>Zaccaria dal Pozzo, an Italian physician.</note>, *The Spagyric Key*. <note>original: "Clavis Spagirica." The term "Spagyric" refers to alchemical medicine, specifically the process of separating and then recombining the essential components of a substance.</note>

**Denis Zachaire** of France, *On the Chemical Miracle* (along with **Trevisan**), confirmed by various authorities of the masters of this art—**Democritus**, **Geber**, **Lull**, and **Villanova**—edited by Gerard Dorn, Basel, 1583.

By the same author, *A Small Work on the Natural Philosophy of Metals*, with annotations by **Nicolas Flamel**, in the *Chemical Theater*. <note>original: "Theatrum Chimicum." This was the most comprehensive collection of alchemical texts published in the 17th century.</note>
**Zachaire** and **[Bernard of] Trevisan**, in French, at Antwerp, 1567, in octavo.
The same, along with *The Fountain of the Lovers of Science*, *The Lament of Nature*, and *The Summary of Flamel*, etc. There are many other various French editions of these.
**Zadith**. See **Senior**. <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, usually referred to by the Latin name "Senior," was an influential 10th-century Arab alchemist.</note>
**Zadith, son of Hamuel**, *The Chemical Table*; it appears among the most ancient writings on *Chemical Philosophy*, Frankfurt, 1605, in octavo, and in the *Chemical Theater*.
**Zalento**. See **Zeleucus**.

## THE CHEMICAL LIBRARY OF PIERRE BOREL.

<note>Pierre Borel (c. 1620–1671) was a French polymath, physician to King Louis XIV, and a diligent collector of scientific and alchemical knowledge. His *Bibliotheca Chimica*, published in 1654, was one of the first comprehensive bibliographies of alchemical books.</note>

SO THAT NOTHING IN THIS LIBRARY
*might seem to be lacking, and so that the work might exist as perfect as possible, since after a new investigation of authors, we have found many more; we have arranged an alphabetical Appendix of them, and have taken care to place it at the end of the Library for the sake of the curious.*

Albenagri <note>A Latinized name likely referring to an early Arabic alchemical author.</note> the Philosopher, *The Marrow of Alchemy*. <note>original: "medulla Alchimiæ"</note>
Master <note>original: "D." for "Dominus," a title of respect for a learned scholar or gentleman.</note> Nathan Albineus <note>Also known as Nathan d’Aubigné (1601–1669), a French-Swiss physician and author of alchemical collections.</note>, *Chemical Library*.

Geber. See Geber. <note>original: "Ieber. Vide Geberum." Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early Islamic chemistry, though many Latin works under his name are now attributed to a "Pseudo-Geber."</note>

Book of the Nine Judges, containing within itself five hundred questions. <note>original: "Liber 9. Iudicum, in ſe continens quæſtiones quingentas."</note>

*John Baptist Montanus of Verona’s* work in 18 books on metallic medicines to be prepared by the Alchemical art.
*By the same author:* Another work, on Sublimations. <note>Sublimation is a chemical process where a solid is heated into a gas and then condensed back into a solid, often used to purify substances like sulfur or mercury.</note>
*Morienus’s* dialogue with *King Khalid* concerning the Philosopher’s Stone. <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit; the "Dialogue of Morienus and Khalid" is one of the earliest known alchemical texts translated from Arabic into Latin.</note>

## Z

The same [Paracelsus], *On Tartaric Diseases, Causes, and Signs* <note>original: "De Tartari morbis"; "Tartar" was a term Paracelsus used for mineral precipitates in the body, which he blamed for conditions like gout and stones</note>, translated by Adam von Bodenstein <note>An early and influential promoter of Paracelsian medicine</note>, Basel, 1563, in octavo <note>original: "in 8."; a standard book size of the period</note>.

By the same, *Exposition of the Images found at Nuremberg, Derived from the Prophecy of True Magic* <note>original: "Expoſitio imaginum Nurembergiae repertarum"; a work of political and spiritual prophecy based on a series of mysterious drawings</note>, 1570, in octavo.

*The Great Surgery of Paracelsus* <note>original: "Grande Chirurgie de Paracelſe"; his most successful work, which revolutionized wound care by arguing against the use of harsh ointments</note>, translated by Hassard, at Antwerp, 1568, in octavo.

The same, *On the Mercuries of Metals* <note>original: "De Mercuriis metallorum"</note>, Basel, 1582, in octavo.

*Experiments of Paracelsus*, with Rouilliasco and Isaac <note>Isaac Hollandus, a name associated with famous Dutch alchemical writings</note> on the vegetable and animal work, by Penot <note>Bernard Georges Penot, a tireless researcher of alchemical medicine</note>, 1582, in octavo.

By the same, *Labyrinth of Errant Physicians* <note>original: "Labyrinthus medicorum errantium"; a polemic arguing that medical truth is found in nature, not in ancient Greek textbooks</note>.

The same, *On the Spirit of Plants, from Occult Philosophy*, 1574, in octavo, Basel.

*The Aurora of Paracelsus* <note>original: "Aurora Paracelſi"</note>, with the *Physical Monarchy* and the *Living Anatomy of Paracelsus*, 1577, in octavo, Basel.

Dorn’s *Dictionary of Paracelsus* <note>original: "Dornei dictionarium Paracelſi"; Gerard Dorn was a vital interpreter who translated Paracelsus’s difficult German and invented jargon into Latin</note>, 1584, in octavo, Frankfurt.

*Errors of a Stranger in his Country, concerning the Brothers of the Rose Cross* <note>original: "Peregrini in patria errores de Fratr. Roſ. Crucis"; a text related to the Rosicrucian movement, a secret society of doctors and sages</note>, Eutopia <note>A common pseudonym for a printing location to avoid censorship, literally meaning "Good Place"</note>, 1618, in duodecimo <note>original: "in 12."; a smaller, more portable book size</note>.

It highlights the work of major editors and translators like Bodenstein and Dorn who helped spread Paracelsian ideas across Europe.</summary>

# PIERRE BOREL’S
## CHEMICAL EPISTLE. <note>Pierre Borel (c. 1620–1671) was a French polymath and royal physician to King Louis XIV, known for his works on medicine, chemistry, and bibliography.</note>

->TO MASTER THOMAS DE RIOLET<-
->Doctor of Medicine of Saintes<- <note>original: "Xantoni"; referring to the town of Saintes or the Saintonge region of France.</note>

Since you have promised me more than once (my dearest friend) an explanation of the emblem of the **Rosicrucian** Brothers <note>original: "Fratrum Roseæ Crucis"; a secret society of mystics and alchemists who claimed to possess ancient wisdom.</note> found in **Maier’s** <note>Michael Maier (1568–1622), a celebrated German alchemist and counselor to Emperor Rudolf II.</note> work *The Golden Themis* <note>original: "Themide aurea"; a book published in 1618 defending the Rosicrucian Order.</note>, as well as the couplet <note>original: "Distichumque"; a poem consisting of two lines.</note> contained within it, and also what was contained in the sealed paper given to you long ago by a Rosicrucian Brother who is your friend—granted under an oath that you would not open it until your twenty-fifth year—and since you have now reached this age and are mindful of your promise, I ask these things of you again, in exchange for which I will share other things with you in turn. Meanwhile,

<header>CHEMICAL LETTERS.</header>

---

## The Unlocking of Maier’s Enigma, in *The Golden Themis*.

Since I have been quite successful in the unlocking of secret ciphers <note>original: "Ciphrarum occultarum"; the 17th century saw a fascination with cryptography as a way to hide scientific and mystical discoveries.</note>—indeed, I have opened even certain ones written in Venetian ciphers, or the so-called "square" <note>The "square" refers to the *Tabula Recta*, a tool used in the Vigenère cipher, which was considered the "undecipherable cipher" for centuries.</note>, though they were previously held to be undecipherable (since the key must be known) by Giambattista della Porta <note>An Italian polymath and cryptographer (1535–1615) known for his work *De Furtivis Literarum Notis*.</note>, Vigenère <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a French diplomat whose cipher remained a standard for secure communication.</note>, and others—I devoted my labor to uncovering the Maierian Enigma in *The Golden Themis* <note>original: "Themide aurea"; a book published by Michael Maier in 1618 defending the Rosicrucian Order.</note>, because I believed great things were contained within it. At last, though not without effort, I unraveled it, for he only swapped half of the letters. It stands thus:

### Maier’s Enigma.

CLode No Marri in ium dicsit vdaoltan plesaritto, Icait os vperrimit cegmusiemon tus polcopitto, im oe igmon cemsu musalun, im hec musaluron os iminusaluron. <note>This string is a transposition cipher. When decoded according to Borel's method, the Latin yields a set of moral instructions: "Cole Deum, ama proximum, fac quod vis, patiere quod debes" (Worship God, love your neighbor, do what you will, suffer what you must).</note>

<summary>Pierre Borel explains how he decoded a famous cipher from Michael Maier’s Rosicrucian text, *Themis Aurea*, noting his expertise in advanced cryptographic methods like the Vigenère square.</summary>
<keywords>Michael Maier, Themis Aurea, cryptography, Giambattista della Porta, Blaise de Vigenère, Rosicrucianism, alchemical cipher, secret codes</keywords>

--- Page 308 ---
<meta>This page concludes the decoding of the Maierian Enigma mentioned on page 275. Pierre Borel provides the "Explicatio" or the plain-text meaning resulting from the transposition cipher he unraveled.</meta>

<page-num>276</page-num>
<header>Explanation.</header>

I believe that I have brought forth nothing contrary to what has already been said, having sufficiently perceived the kinship of Jupiter and Apollo <note>In alchemical symbolism, Jupiter and Apollo (the Sun) represent specific metals—tin and gold—or specific stages of the transformation of matter. Their "kinship" refers to the underlying unity of the material being worked upon.</note>; in the former <note>referring to Jupiter</note> there is a fire against nature <note>original: "ignem contra naturam"; in alchemy, "fire against nature" often refers to a corrosive substance, such as an acid or "strong water," that dissolves the substance to begin the process of purification.</note>, while in the latter <note>referring to Apollo or the Sun</note> there is a fire both natural and unnatural <note>Natural fire refers to the gentle, life-giving heat used in the "Great Work," while unnatural fire refers to a heat that can destroy the spirit of the matter if not carefully regulated.</note>.

->THE END.<-

<summary>This page provides the decoded meaning of Michael Maier’s alchemical enigma, focusing on the symbolic "fires" associated with the figures of Jupiter and Apollo. It concludes Borel's technical explanation of the cipher.</summary>

<keywords>alchemical fire, Jupiter, Apollo, Michael Maier, The Golden Themis, Pierre Borel, fire against nature, transmutation</keywords>
